name: Toyota Grand Highlander Hybrid XLE
why: Scores the maximum 5 on four qualitative criteria simultaneously: car seat fit, 3rd row comfort, corridor performance, and reliability. No other candidate achieves this combination. The 3rd row offers 39.5" of legroom — genuinely adult-comfortable on a 2-hour corridor drive — while the standard 8-seat bench accommodates three car seats comfortably. Toyota's #1 Consumer Reports reliability rating and the 10-year/240,000 km hybrid battery warranty make this the lowest-risk long-hold ownership proposition. The new vehicle's horizon-end residual projection (~$27,000) significantly exceeds the used version's (~$13,000) — the source of its TCO advantage.
tradeoffs: At ~$62,700 on-road it is the most expensive new purchase in this comparison. Fuel costs of ~$16,900 over the planning horizon are substantially higher than PHEV and BEV alternatives (~$9,000–11,500 more). No plug-in capability. Whether the horizon-end residual projections are reliable enough to justify buying new over the used version (rank 2) is a legitimate question — the ~$10,000 purchase price gap is real cash today; the residual difference is a projection.

name: Toyota Sienna Hybrid XLE AWD

specs.third_row_legroom: Comfortable for kids; short trips for adults

why: Same Sienna Hybrid platform as the used candidate at rank 3, with two material upgrades for a long-hold: full 10-year/240,000 km hybrid battery warranty starts fresh from purchase (used 2022–23 examples have 6–7 yrs remaining), and the horizon-end residual projection is materially higher (~$23k vs ~$11k for the used). The premium over the used version is ~$7k on-road; whether that's worth it depends on how much weight you put on the warranty tail and the residual delta.
tradeoffs: Highest on-road price of any minivan in the comparison. Ground clearance of 170 mm is among the lowest in the field. The minivan format limits FSR utility (sliding doors and low body are highway/urban features). Same fuel economy as the used Sienna Hybrid; no electrification beyond the hybrid system.

name: Toyota Grand Highlander Hybrid XLE
why: Qualitative scores are identical to the new version across every criterion — same vehicle, same capabilities. The gap from rank 1 is entirely due to a lower TCO score, reflecting a higher net TCO driven by a lower projected horizon-end residual on a used vehicle. At ~$52,400 on-road versus ~$62,700 new, the lower purchase price is real and substantial.
tradeoffs: Same qualitative trade-offs as rank 1: high fuel cost vs PHEV/BEV, no plug-in, towing requires Hybrid MAX trim (verify at purchase). Hybrid battery warranty transfer should be verified at point of sale. A 2023–24 example will be 11–13 years old at the end of the ownership horizon. This is the better choice if you are sceptical of horizon-end residual projections or prefer to avoid the premium of buying new.
caution: Verify Toyota 10yr/240,000km hybrid battery warranty transfer at purchase.

name: Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid Touring L
why: The only PHEV minivan available in the comparison — 51 km of EV range covers most Metro Vancouver daily driving on home electricity, and the 10-year/240,000 km Stellantis traction-battery warranty has ~7 yrs left at purchase. Sliding doors + flat floor + genuine adult-friendly 3rd row are the minivan structural advantages. 8-year/160k km PHEV component warranty is U.S. only — in Canada the Stellantis warranty is 8yr/130k on hybrid system + 10yr/240k on battery.
tradeoffs: Stellantis reliability is a real concern — Consumer Reports rates the Pacifica below average, with electrical-system complaints concentrated in the hybrid version. Cargo is excellent but ground clearance of 130 mm is the lowest in this field — FSR use is not on the table. FWD only (no AWD on Pacifica Hybrid). Used supply in BC is thin.
caution: Pacifica Hybrid Canadian warranty is 8yr/130k on hybrid drive + 10yr/240k on traction battery. Verify both at purchase, plus any open recalls (early 22 hybrids had a software stop-sale that's since been resolved).

name: Toyota Sienna Hybrid Woodland AWD

specs.third_row_legroom: Comfortable for kids; short trips for adults

why: Scores the maximum 5 on car seat fit, cargo utility, and corridor performance. The sliding rear doors are a daily convenience with young children that no SUV in this comparison matches. Cargo at 949 L behind the third row is nearly double the Sorento PHEV. Fuel economy at ~6.5 L/100km is the best non-plug-in vehicle here, producing a ~1,077 km tank range. Toyota #1 reliability and 10-year/240,000 km hybrid battery warranty.
tradeoffs: Ground clearance of 160–175 mm is the lowest of all 12 candidates — a highway and urban vehicle; FSR use is not recommended. The minivan format is a personal preference — functionally it is the most practical layout for a family of five with young children.
caution: Verify Toyota 10yr/240,000km hybrid battery warranty transfer at purchase.

name: Honda Odyssey EX-L / Touring
why: The ICE minivan benchmark. Magic Slide 2nd row genuinely solves three-car-seat geometry better than any SUV in this comparison — the centre seat can offset or remove without disturbing the outboards, making a clear walkthrough to the 3rd row. Adult-friendly 3rd row, 929 L cargo behind it, Honda's strong reliability record on this generation, and the largest used supply of any minivan candidate in BC.
tradeoffs: FWD only — no AWD ever offered on the Odyssey. Fuel costs of ~$22k over the planning horizon are typical for a V6 minivan. Ground clearance of 115 mm is the lowest in the entire field — strictly a highway/urban vehicle. No hybrid or electrified Odyssey in this generation. Factory powertrain warranty expires by 2027 on most used examples.

name: Subaru Ascent Touring AWD

specs.third_row_legroom: Tight for adults; fine for children

why: Scores the maximum 5 on corridor performance, hitch compatibility, reliability, and FSR capability. The FSR score of 5 is unique — 221 mm ground clearance with Subaru's Symmetrical full-time AWD and X-Mode terrain management is the most capable system in this comparison. Subaru ranks #2 at Consumer Reports. Lowest purchase price in the comparison (~$38,500 on-road).
tradeoffs: Fuel costs of ~$23,000 over the planning horizon are among the highest — ICE-only with no electrification path. The 3rd row is tight for adults. Factory warranty exhausted on 2022–23 examples.

name: Kia Carnival SX / SX+
why: Kia's reinterpretation of the minivan as a unibody MPV — slightly higher ride height than the Odyssey/Pacifica (170 mm vs 115–130) and the most cargo capacity of any vehicle in this comparison at 1,135 L behind the third row. Adult-friendly 3rd row, sliding doors, 8-seat configuration on SX trim. Lowest purchase price of any minivan candidate.
tradeoffs: FWD only — same AWD-absent constraint as Odyssey and Pacifica. 2022–23 reliability is mid-pack (Kia brand has improved but the Carnival's first-generation transmission and electronics have an unsettled record). 5yr/100k powertrain warranty expires by 2027 on most used examples. Factory hitch is a dealer-install option on SX trim — verify or budget aftermarket.
caution: First-generation Carnival (2022+); some early production had electrical-system complaints. Verify recall history at purchase.

name: Toyota Highlander Hybrid XLE AWD
why: Toyota #1 reliability and the 10-year/240,000 km hybrid battery warranty at the lowest purchase price of any Toyota hybrid in this comparison. Note: this is the standard Highlander, NOT the Grand Highlander — a smaller vehicle.
tradeoffs: The 3rd row scores a 2 — approximately 30" of legroom, comfortable for children but not suitable for adults on a 2-hour corridor run. This is why it ranks below both Grand Highlander variants despite better TCO. Towing is 3,500 lbs. Verify 8-seat bench availability on XLE trim at purchase.
caution: Standard Highlander — NOT the Grand Highlander. Smaller interior and tighter 3rd row. Verify 8-seat bench and hybrid battery warranty transfer at purchase.

name: Hyundai Palisade Preferred/Urban AWD
why: The most affordable way to get a genuinely adult-friendly 3rd row in this comparison at ~$40,700 on-road. Interior quality is widely regarded as the most refined of any non-luxury 3-row SUV at this price. AWD is standard on all Canadian trims. Strong Vancouver supply with 45+ listings within 50 km.
tradeoffs: Fuel costs of ~$24,000 over the planning horizon are the joint highest. Reliability rated 'average' at Consumer Reports. A wiper motor recall affects 2021–2024 models — verify completion at purchase. No hybrid option in this generation.
caution: Wiper motor recall affects 2021–2024 models (failure in ice/snow buildup). Verify recall completion before purchase.

name: Kia Telluride EX AWD
why: The segment benchmark. Scores 5 on car seat fit, corridor performance, and hitch compatibility, and a 4 on 3rd row comfort. Consumer Reports rates the Telluride above the Kia brand average. 5,500 lb tow rating leads the field. Build quality is a genuine benchmark for the segment.
tradeoffs: Highest net TCO in the cohort, driven almost entirely by ~$24,000 in fuel costs over the planning horizon. The Telluride is the right choice if 3rd row adult comfort and driving experience are weighted heavily enough to justify the running cost premium.

name: Tesla Model Y Long Range AWD

specs.third_row_legroom: No 3rd row (2023+ Model Y is 5-seat only in Canada)

why: Same constraints and benefits as the new Model Y at a much lower entry price (~$50k on-road vs ~$73k). Traction-battery warranty has ~6 years remaining on 2023–24 examples (8yr/192k from in-service date). Strong used supply in BC compared to other BEVs.
tradeoffs: Same five-seat constraint as the new version. Used Tesla resale weakened materially through 2024–25 — projected horizon-end residual is one of the lowest in the field as a percentage of purchase price. Battery health (and any warranty service history) varies widely on used examples; insist on the Service Mode battery health report at purchase.
caution: Five-seat only. Confirm remaining traction-battery warranty and request a Service Mode battery-degradation report from the dealer before purchase.

name: Honda Pilot EX-L/Touring AWD
why: Unique removable/stowable second-row centre seat: 8-seat bench with latch removal in under 30 seconds, creating a clear walkthrough lane to the 3rd row without disturbing car seats. Honda CPO certification (7yr/160K warranty) may be available. Honda top-tier reliability. Ground clearance of 220 mm is second-highest in the comparison.
tradeoffs: ICE only — no hybrid Pilot in Canada. Fuel costs of ~$22,000 over the planning horizon. 3rd row is tight for adults on longer trips. This vehicle is likely undervalued by the matrix — the removable centre seat is a practical daily feature the scoring doesn't fully capture.
caution: 2023 or newer ONLY. The 2022 Pilot is a prior-generation vehicle — do not confuse them.

name: Kia Sorento PHEV EX
why: Among the lowest net TCO in the cohort. A 57 km electric range covers most Vancouver daily driving on home electricity, while 710 km combined range eliminates corridor anxiety. Fuel and energy costs (~$7,100 over the planning horizon) are dramatically lower than any ICE candidate.
tradeoffs: 3rd row is children-only — a structural limitation no trim resolves. Cargo at 357 L behind the third row is the smallest of all candidates. Tow rating 1,654 lbs. If 3rd row is genuinely children-only for you, this vehicle's low TCO may warrant reconsideration despite ranking 9th.
caution: Verify PHEV battery warranty transferability at purchase. 3rd row is children-only — not suitable for adult passengers.

name: Mazda CX-90 PHEV GS
why: TCO score of 3.77 (second best in the field). Good qualitative scores on car seat fit, winter capability, and FSR. 8-seat bench standard on all trims. Premium interior quality. 203 mm clearance with i-ACTIV AWD.
tradeoffs: Reliability score of 1 — Consumer Reports rates 'well below average' in its second model year. This is the primary risk for a long-hold ownership horizon. 3.3 kW onboard charger takes ~6 hours for full charge. Thin BC used supply.
caution: Consumer Reports 'well-below average' reliability in year 2. Significant risk for long-hold ownership. Verify carefully at purchase.

name: Kia EV9 Land AWD
why: Scores maximum 5 on hitch compatibility. 800V/350 kW charging recovers ~1,000 km of range per hour. Low energy costs over the planning horizon (~$4,900) — among the cheapest to fuel in the cohort. Kia won Canadian Black Book Best Retained Value for BEV SUVs.
tradeoffs: Car seat fit scores a 3 (bench tight with three car seats). On-road price of ~$62,100 is the highest used candidate. Unknown battery history — verify warranty status. Will be 10+ years old by the end of a default-horizon hold — first-generation EV risk. Requires one planned charging stop Vancouver–Kamloops.
caution: Used BEV: verify battery health history and remaining warranty coverage before purchase.

name: Tesla Model Y Long Range AWD

specs.third_row_legroom: No 3rd row (2023+ Model Y is 5-seat only in Canada)

why: Included for benchmarking, not as a family-fit recommendation: best-in-class fast-charging via Supercharger, ~17 kWh/100km efficiency yields the lowest fuel cost of any candidate, and Tesla's drivetrain warranty (8yr/192k km traction battery) covers the cliff years of this hold. If two-row seating with cargo is sufficient, this is the easiest BEV ownership in the comparison.
tradeoffs: Five seats only — 2023+ Canadian Model Ys do not offer the optional 3rd row, so three car seats across the back row is a structural daily constraint with no overflow capacity for guests. Reliability scores 3 (Consumer Reports rates 'average' with persistent panel-gap and trim complaints on this generation). No hitch from the factory in Canada — accessory hitch (1.25" or 2") is dealer-fit. Highest insurance premium of any candidate.
caution: Five-seat only. If a 6th or 7th passenger is ever required, this vehicle does not fit the family.

name: Hyundai IONIQ 9 Preferred AWD
why: Best BEV 3rd row in the comparison (score 4), widest interior, 539 km of range, 800V/350 kW charging. May be the most compelling BEV to revisit in 2027 once reliability data accumulates and used examples appear.
tradeoffs: First-year model with no reliability history — score 2. TCO score of 2.01 near top of range due to $75,100 purchase price. Ground clearance of 177 mm is the lowest of all 12 candidates. Not the right choice to buy new today, but worth watching for a 2027 used purchase.
caution: First-year model (2026) — no reliability history. Consider waiting for 2027 used examples with established track record.

name: Toyota bZ4X AWD

specs.range_km: 388 km rated (100 kW DCFC peak, CCS)

why: Toyota's first BEV at a heavily-discounted entry price (~$28k–$40k used in BC, well below any other BEV in the cohort). Toyota brand serviceability + parts ubiquity tilt the OOW repair tail in its favour vs Korean BEVs / Tesla. Surprisingly generous ground clearance (215 mm) for a road crossover. Lowest net TCO in the cohort at the default 10yr horizon despite the steep residual write-down. The 2023–24 AWD examples have ~5 yrs left on the 8yr/160k traction-battery warranty (NOT the 10yr Toyota hybrid warranty — important distinction).
tradeoffs: 5-seat structural constraint same as Tesla Model Y — three car seats across one row works but there is zero overflow for a guest. Pre-refresh 100 kW DCFC peak + weak cold-weather charging preconditioning was the loudest review complaint: Vancouver–Kamloops needs two charging stops in winter. 388 km nominal range degrades materially in winter. Hitch is a low-capacity (1500 lbs) dealer-fit accessory. Toyota's BEV warranty is the BEV industry baseline (8yr/160k), not the 10yr/240k that the hybrids enjoy — do not over-rate the brand moat.
caution: Verify completion of the 2022 wheel-hub recall on any 2023 example. Confirm remaining 8yr/160k traction-battery warranty at point of purchase. Five-seat only.

name: Toyota bZ XLE AWD
why: 2026 "bZ" refresh is a meaningful update over the used bZ4X: 77 kWh battery (up from 71), 468 km range (up from 388), 150 kW DCFC peak (up from 100), NACS port giving Tesla Supercharger access, 11 kW onboard AC charger, and a standard heat pump improving winter efficiency. Toyota's brand reliability + parts network is the strongest moat among BEVs in the cohort — a structural advantage at the 8-year OOW cliff that Korean BEVs and Tesla can't match. Full 8yr/160k traction-battery warranty from purchase covers the entire planning horizon.
tradeoffs: Still 5-seat only — same structural family-of-five constraint as Tesla Model Y. MSRP $53,390 (XLE AWD) lands the on-road around $62,500 — cheaper than Model Y LR new ($73k) but more than every other BEV used in the cohort. Range and charging speed are now competitive, but no longer the leader: 800V Korean BEVs (EV9, IONIQ 9) still charge faster and Tesla still has the Supercharger density. Towing 1500 lbs and accessory-only hitch are the same weaknesses as the used bZ4X. Toyota's BEV warranty is 8yr/160k, NOT the 10yr hybrid moat — the brand moat narrows once you leave hybrids.
caution: Five-seat only. The 8yr/160k battery warranty is the BEV industry baseline, not the 10yr hybrid coverage — do not transfer the Toyota-hybrid mental model to this vehicle.

name: Honda Pilot EX-L AWD
why: The 10-year vintage pick: a full 8-seat 3-row SUV for the price of a used compact. The EX-L AWD's 6-speed automatic avoids the troublesome 9-speed ZF that the Touring/Elite trims got — a deliberate trim choice for reliability. Cheap entry ($18.5k on-road), 5,000 lb towing, and proper 8-passenger capacity make it the most family-capable vehicle here per dollar of purchase price.
tradeoffs: Cheap to buy, expensive to keep: out of warranty entirely, so ~$34k of expected maintenance + repairs over a 10yr hold dominates its TCO. Fuel costs ~$24k (V6, ~11 L/100km). Reliability scores 3 — the 2016 (first year of the 3rd gen) carried connecting-rod-bearing and fuel-tank-weld recalls; verify both are closed. 3rd row is kid-only. By the end of a long hold it's a 20-year-old vehicle.
caution: First year of the 3rd-gen Pilot. Verify the connecting-rod-bearing and fuel-tank recalls are closed, and that it's an EX-L (6-spd), not a 9-spd Touring/Elite.

name: Toyota Sienna LE AWD
why: The 15-year vintage pick, and a quietly excellent BC choice: the 3rd-gen Sienna is the only AWD minivan ever sold, which on the Coquihalla in winter matters more than any SUV's marketing. Owners rate it 4.6/5 for reliability and maintenance cost is famously low for the class. Sliding doors + flat floor + 7 seats + 1,107 L of cargo deliver more usable family space than anything else at this $13.5k entry price.
tradeoffs: Out of warranty, ~15 years old: ~$42k of expected maintenance over a full 10yr hold is the largest single TCO component, and AWD driveline service (PTU, transfer, runflat-era suspension) adds to the tail. Fuel ~$26.5k (V6, no electrification). Ground clearance of 115 mm is the lowest in the entire field — strictly pavement + packed snow, no FSR. Residual approaches scrap by the end of a long hold.
caution: 15-year-old AWD minivan: budget for driveline/suspension wear. Confirm AWD system service history and check for the runflat-to-conventional tire conversion (common, fine).

name: Volkswagen Atlas Highline 3.6 VR6 4MOTION

specs.third_row_legroom: Roomy — among the best non-minivan 3rd rows for car seats

why: The 5-year vintage pick, chosen for space: the Atlas has one of the roomiest 3rd rows of any midsize SUV — it genuinely seats car seats in row 3, with three-across capability in the wide 2nd row, so it 'for sure' carries five car seats. 4MOTION AWD suits BC winters, and at ~$32k on-road it is the cheapest comfortable 3-row in the field. The gas-VW counterpart to the ID. Buzz for an apples-to-apples brand read.
tradeoffs: Volkswagen reliability is the weak point — below-average on the data, scoring 2, and it is fully out of warranty (VW's 4yr/80k comprehensive expired in 2025), so the expected repair tail is the highest of any non-luxury vehicle here. The VR6 is thirsty (~12 L/100km, ~$24k fuel). Depreciation has been steep, which is good for buying and bad for resale.
caution: VW reliability/electronics are the risk. Insist on full service history; check cooling system, DSG behaviour, and infotainment/electronics for faults at purchase.

name: Toyota Sequoia SR5 V8 4WD

specs.third_row_legroom: Full-size 8-seat; 3rd row OK for adults on short trips

why: The 20-year vintage pick — and the only old-iron survivor with a real third row. The 1st-gen Sequoia's 4.7L 2UZ-FE V8 is one of the most durable engines Toyota ever built (owners rate this generation 4.8/5 at 20 years). Body-on-frame, 4WD with low range, 250 mm clearance: maxes both winter and FSR (5/5, only the retired 4Runner pick matched it) while seating 8 and towing 6,200 lbs. Keeps the rugged story but adds the third row the family needs.
tradeoffs: Thirstiest vehicle in the entire cohort: ~16 L/100km gives it ~$32k of fuel over a 10yr hold, and combined with ~$40k of expected maintenance on a 20-year-old truck, the running cost dwarfs the cheap $15k entry. Trucky ride, ~520 km range means frequent fuel stops on the corridor. Only worth it if winter/FSR capability is weighted above almost everything.
caution: 20-year-old vehicle. Verify the lower-ball-joint recall was completed, inspect frame/suspension, and budget for age-related wear despite the bulletproof V8.

name: Volkswagen ID. Buzz 1st Edition 4MOTION
why: The only electric vehicle in the cohort with a truly adult-friendly 3rd row (VW claims industry-leading legroom) and three-across 2nd-row car-seat capability — a 7-seat BEV that 'for sure' fits five car seats. 4MOTION AWD for BC winters, a vast flat load floor, and the most distinctive design here. Sets the electric-3-row benchmark.
tradeoffs: 373 km of rated range is short for a $94k vehicle this size, and the ~2,900 kg curb weight means real-world highway range drops further — the Vancouver–Kamloops corridor needs a planned charging stop with thin winter margin (corridor scores 2). First-year VW MEB-platform BEV with no reliability track record and a history of software gremlins (reliability 2). Tows only 2,400 lbs. Highest on-road price in the field.
caution: First-year model on VW's MEB platform — budget for software/electronics teething. Verify the corridor range works for your trips before committing.

name: Volkswagen ID. Buzz 1st Edition 4MOTION
why: The same electric 7-seat at a steep first-year depreciation discount — roughly $22k off the new price. If you want the only adult-friendly electric 3rd row in the field and can live with the unproven platform, the used 1st Edition is the value way in, and it still has ~7 yrs of the 8yr/160k battery warranty.
tradeoffs: Same short 373 km range, thin corridor margin, and first-year MEB reliability question as the new one (reliability 2). Novelty BEVs can keep depreciating, so the resale picture is uncertain. Battery-health verification is essential on any used EV.
caution: Used first-year BEV: get a battery-health report and confirm remaining 8yr/160k traction-battery warranty before purchase.

name: Honda CR-V EX AWD
powertrain: ICE — 2.4L I4, Real Time AWD (current car, ~19yr)
why: The household's CURRENT vehicle — included as the 'keep what we have' baseline, not a shopping candidate. There's no purchase price to pay (you already own it), so the forward 10-year cost is almost entirely fuel + age-related maintenance against a near-zero residual. In absolute dollars that 'do nothing' cost is low, which is exactly why it's worth seeing on the board: every upgrade has to justify its premium over simply keeping this. The reason it IS on the shopping list: it's a 5-seat compact, and three car seats across its rear bench is the daily squeeze driving the search for a third row.
tradeoffs: 5-seat, no third row — the core limitation pushing the upgrade (cannot 'for sure' fit five car seats). At ~19 years old the maintenance line dominates its TCO and will only climb; ~9.5 L/100km and a ~600 km tank make corridor trips workable but dated. Real Time AWD + 185 mm clearance handle BC winters adequately but it's no FSR tool. Honda reliability (4) is the redeeming trait — these 3rd-gen CR-Vs routinely pass 300,000 km.
caution: 19-year-old vehicle: the upgrade case is about space and safety-tech, not a mechanical cliff. Watch the AWD rear-differential fluid service interval and A/C compressor, the known 3rd-gen wear items.

name: Hyundai Palisade Luxury Hybrid AWD
why: The fully redesigned 2026 Palisade Luxury arrives with Hyundai's new 2.5T parallel-hybrid system (329 hp combined) replacing the old 3.8L V6. NRCan rates it 8.1 L/100km combined — a ~3 L/100km improvement on the outgoing 3.8L. Standard AWD across all trims, 8-seat configuration, refined interior, and a full 8yr/160k traction-battery warranty from purchase. The non-Toyota new-hybrid 3-row alternative to the Grand Highlander Hybrid.
tradeoffs: First-year-of-redesign reliability is unknown (scored 3) — Hyundai brand reliability is industry-average but this is an all-new hybrid system on a new platform. At ~$74,500 on-road it is $11.8k more than the Grand Highlander Hybrid new, and 8.1 L/100km is ~17% thirstier than Toyota's hybrid (6.9 L). Towing capacity drops to 4,000 lbs on the hybrid trim (the gas trim tows 5,000). Third-row legroom of 32.1" is kid-friendly but tight for adults — well below the Grand Highlander's 39.5".
caution: First model year of an all-new hybrid system on a redesigned platform. Wait for first reliability data unless dealer support and warranty terms address the risk.

name: Volkswagen Atlas SEL Premium R-Line 4MOTION

specs.third_row_legroom: Adult-friendly 3rd row — among the roomiest in class

why: The refreshed (2024-on) 4-cylinder Atlas at top-trim SEL Premium R-Line 4MOTION: one of the roomiest 3rd rows in the class, three-across 2nd-row bench for car seats (scores 5 on car-seat fit), 5,000-lb towing, and 4MOTION AWD standard at this trim. VW's 4yr/80,000km comprehensive warranty is the longest bumper-to-bumper coverage among the new ICE 3-rows here. The non-Toyota, non-Hyundai, non-Kia new 3-row option — useful as a brand baseline against the Korean and Japanese hybrid contenders.
tradeoffs: VW reliability is the headline risk: brand reliability scores below-average industry-wide (matrix score 2), and although the 2.0T + 8-speed swap to a single drivetrain simplifies the lineup, the broader VW repair tail still dominates the model's OOW cost projection. At ~$66,200 on-road plus ~11 L/100km fuel (~$23k over the planning horizon) and steep VW depreciation, the 10-year net TCO is the highest in the entire field — ahead of even the ID. Buzz new. The 269 hp 2.0T is adequate but a step down from the discontinued VR6.
caution: VW reliability/electronics are the structural risk. The 4yr/80k comprehensive warranty is the longest among new ICE 3-rows but expires before the cliff years; consider VW's extended-warranty options at purchase.

name: Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid Touring L (PHEV, FWD)
why: The new (dealer-quoted $70,000) version of the Pacifica Hybrid you test-drove. Same PHEV powertrain, but fresh: full 10yr/240k traction-battery warranty from purchase covers the entire planning horizon (the used 2022-23 has ~7 yrs left). The Stow-N-Go 2nd-row bench is REPLACED by removable captain's chairs on the PHEV (battery occupies the under-floor wells) — the 3rd-row Stow-N-Go you liked is unchanged. FWD only — no AWD on the hybrid.
tradeoffs: ~$31k more on-road than the 2022-23 used Pacifica Hybrid (~$39k). Stellantis brand reliability is below-average (score 3), and the steep first-year depreciation on a $70k minivan eats into the resale. No AWD — winter score 3 (vs the gas AWD's 4). Ground clearance 130 mm — pavement vehicle. The big gain over the used: 10 fresh years of battery warranty.
caution: Confirm Canadian warranty terms (Stellantis Canada: 8yr/130k on hybrid system + 10yr/240k on traction battery). Verify no open recalls/stop-sales on the model year.

name: Chrysler Pacifica Touring L AWD
why: The only AWD minivan currently sold (alongside the Toyota Sienna Hybrid AWD) — dealer-quoted at $66,225. Keeps the gas Pacifica's full Stow-N-Go capability (BOTH 2nd-row bench AND 3rd row fold into the floor — the PHEV loses 2nd-row Stow-N-Go to the battery pack). 287 hp Pentastar V6 + 9-speed, factory hitch, 3,600 lb towing. The non-hybrid minivan answer if you want AWD without giving up the Stow-N-Go magic.
tradeoffs: No electrification — ~12 L/100km gives it ~$23.5k of fuel over the planning horizon (3.3× the PHEV's $7.1k). 5yr/100k powertrain warranty (vs the PHEV's 10yr battery), so out-of-warranty maintenance dominates years 6–10 of the TCO model. Stellantis brand reliability average (score 3); industry data on the gas Pacifica V6 is more favourable than the hybrid system but still mid-pack.
caution: Verify the 5yr/100k powertrain warranty terms and any open recalls on the model year. Confirm AWD system service intervals.

name: Kia Carnival Hybrid SX+ FWD
why: The hybrid minivan I missed in the original cohort — launched for 2025 model year, Kia's answer to the Sienna Hybrid. 242 hp combined from 1.6T + electric motor, NRCan-rated ~7.1 L/100km, no plug. FWD-only (no AWD on the hybrid). 8-seat configuration with Kia's full-length VIP-style 2nd row in top trims. The third Korean/Japanese hybrid minivan option alongside Sienna Hybrid and Pacifica Hybrid PHEV.
tradeoffs: FWD-only — winter score 3 (vs Sienna Hybrid AWD's 3 too, so not actually worse on BC roads, but no all-weather edge over the new gas Pacifica AWD). 1.6T-based hybrid system is newer/less proven than Toyota's planetary hybrid — reliability scored 3 (Kia brand-average, first-gen Carnival hybrid). 8yr/160k Kia hybrid-battery warranty is shorter than Toyota's 10yr/240k.
caution: First-gen hybrid powertrain for the Carnival — verify 8yr/160k Kia hybrid-battery warranty terms at purchase. No AWD option on the hybrid.

name: Honda Odyssey Touring
why: The new (2026) gas-only counterpart to the existing used Odyssey, included for new-vs-used comparison within the same nameplate. 280 hp 3.5L V6 + 10-speed auto, FWD-only (Honda has never offered AWD on the Odyssey). Honda reliability (score 4) is the highest among non-Toyota new minivans here. Magic Slide 2nd-row seat lets you reconfigure for daily car-seat access without removing seats.
tradeoffs: FWD-only and 115 mm of ground clearance — the lowest in the active cohort — limit winter and FSR utility (scores 3 and 2). 10.6 L/100km combined gives it ~$23k of fuel over the planning horizon, 3× the Pacifica Hybrid PHEV's $7k. Honda's 5yr/100k powertrain warranty leaves 5 years of cliff-side OOW maintenance — though Honda's repair tail is genuinely cheaper than Stellantis or VW (2.5× ratio applied here).
caution: FWD-only minivan — confirm winter-tire setup is enough for Coquihalla use. Verify Magic Slide seat functionality with your car-seat configuration in-person.

name: Kia Carnival SX FWD
why: The gas-only Carnival — cheapest new minivan on the board at ~$55k on-road. Same body as the Carnival Hybrid (1,139 L cargo behind row 3, 8-seat with available 7-seat captains, the largest minivan cargo here). 290 hp 3.5L V6, 8-speed, FWD. The cross-shop for the gas Pacifica AWD if AWD isn't a hard requirement.
tradeoffs: FWD-only and 173 mm clearance leave winter at 3 / FSR at 2 — the gas Pacifica AWD beats it on all-weather. ~11 L/100km gives it ~$24k of fuel, dwarfing both hybrid alternatives. 5yr/100k powertrain warranty leaves 5 years of cliff-side maintenance. Kia depreciation has been steeper than Toyota's, so the residual gives back less of the cheap entry price.
caution: Verify the 5yr/100k Kia powertrain warranty and any open recalls; the 2022+ Carnival has had a couple of minor recalls.
